## Where we are

- Deck 01: $\pi$ and $\theta_W$ **both** estimate $\theta = 4N_e\mu$ under neutrality +
  constant size.
- When they **disagree**, the neutral-equilibrium null is broken — by **demography** or
  **selection**.
- **Today:** the **site frequency spectrum (SFS)** packages that signal, and **Tajima's
  $D$** reads it.

## Learning objectives

By the end you should be able to:

- Build the SFS from a sample and state its **neutral expectation** $\mathbb E[\xi_i]=\theta/i$.
- Derive **Tajima's $D$** and interpret its sign.
- Explain why **demography is genome-wide** but **selection is local** — and why that
  distinction is everything.
- Describe **linked selection** (sweeps, background selection) and its diversity valley.
- Derive the neutral substitution rate $k=\mu$ and read $d_N/d_S$.

# The coalescent for a sample {.center}

## From a pair to a sample

For $n$ lineages, each **pair** coalesces at rate $1/2N$, and there are $\binom{n}{2}$
pairs, so the wait while $k$ lineages remain is short when $k$ is large:

$$
\mathbb E[T_k] = \frac{2N}{\binom{k}{2}} = \frac{4N}{k(k-1)} .
$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Total branch length summed over all lineages:

$$
\mathbb E[L] = \sum_{k=2}^{n} k\,\mathbb E[T_k] = 2N\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{1}{i} = 2N a_n .
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

shallow tips, short deep internal branches; mutations dropped on branches.

# The site frequency spectrum {.center}

## Definition and neutral expectation

The **SFS** counts segregating sites by the number of copies $i$ of the derived allele in
a sample of $n$. Under the neutral, constant-size coalescent:

$$
\boxed{\;\mathbb E[\xi_i] = \frac{\theta}{i}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n-1\;}
$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- A mutation on a branch subtending $i$ tips appears $i$ times ⟹ rare variants
  (singletons, $i=1$) dominate.
- **Both** diversity estimators are SFS summaries:
  $\theta_W \propto \sum_i \xi_i$ (counts sites equally),
  $\pi \propto \sum_i i(n-i)\,\xi_i$ (weights intermediate frequencies).
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}
**FIGURE** — neutral SFS bar chart: derived-allele count $i$ on x, $\xi_i$ on y, showing
the $1/i$ decline; optionally bottleneck/expansion overlays.
:::

<!-- ALT TEXT (required when the image is added) — pick & refine one,

  A) "Bar chart of the neutral site frequency spectrum where site counts fall off as one over derived-allele frequency, singletons tallest."
  B) "Site frequency spectrum contrasting the neutral expectation with the rare-variant excess of an expanding population."
-->
:::

::::

## Folded vs. unfolded

- **Unfolded** SFS needs an **outgroup** to polarize ancestral vs. derived (often hard in
  plants with messy outgroups / paralogy).
- **Folded** SFS uses the **minor**-allele count $\eta_i = \xi_i + \xi_{n-i}$ — no outgroup
  required, but loses directionality.

::: {.callout-note}
Mispolarization (wrong ancestral allele) inflates the high-frequency-derived class and can
mimic the signal of positive selection — a real hazard in non-model plants.
:::

# Tajima's $D$ {.center}

## Construction

Both $\pi$ and $\theta_W$ estimate $\theta$, so their **difference** is a contrast of the
SFS that vanishes under the null. Tajima standardized it [@tajima1989]:

$$
D = \frac{\pi - \theta_W}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\pi - \theta_W)}} .
$$

- $\pi$ leans on **intermediate**-frequency variants; $\theta_W$ counts **all** segregating
  sites (rare ones included).
- So $D$ asks: is the SFS **rare-skewed** ($\pi < \theta_W$) or
  **intermediate-skewed** ($\pi > \theta_W$)?

## Interpreting the sign

| $D$ | SFS shape | Demographic cause (genome-wide) | Selective cause (local) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $< 0$ | excess rare variants | population **expansion** | recent **sweep**, purifying selection |
| $\approx 0$ | neutral | constant size | neutral |
| $> 0$ | excess intermediate | **bottleneck**, structure | **balancing** selection |

::: {.callout-important}
$D$ alone is **ambiguous** — the same value can come from history or selection. Resolving
it is the next slide.
:::

## Demography vs. selection — the discriminator

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Demography** (bottlenecks, expansions, structure) acts on **every locus** — it shifts
  the **genome-wide** SFS.
- **Selection** acts on **specific loci** and their linked neighborhoods — a **local**
  departure against the genome-wide background.
- ⟹ Build the **genome-wide distribution** of $D$ (or $F_{ST}$), then flag **outliers**.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}

with a localized dip over a selected gene.
:::

## Worked example — maize domestication

Maize was domesticated from **teosinte** ~9,000 ya through a **bottleneck**
[@wright2005maize; @hufford2012maize]:

- **Genome-wide:** the bottleneck lost diversity and skewed the SFS — a demographic
  signature present everywhere.
- **At domestication loci** (e.g. ***tb1***, *teosinte branched1*): a **selective sweep**
  drove a far stronger **local** loss of diversity and strongly **negative** $D$, standing
  out above the genome-wide background.

::: {.callout-tip}
This is the template for crop-origin scans: separate the **demographic** loss (everywhere)
from the **selective** loss (at the genes that matter).
:::

# Linked selection {.center}

## Selection drags its neighbors

Selection acts on one site, but **linkage** spreads the consequences to neutral neighbors —
the dominant force shaping diversity *along* a genome.

- **Selective sweep (hitchhiking):** a favored mutation sweeps to fixation, dragging its
  haplotype and **erasing** nearby diversity — a **valley** in $\pi$ [@smithhaigh1974].
- **Background selection:** purging of linked **deleterious** mutations also removes neutral
  variation, depressing diversity in low-recombination regions [@charlesworth1993].

## How deep and how wide?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
$$
T_{\text{fix}} \approx \frac{2\ln(2N_e)}{s},
\qquad
\text{swept width} \sim \frac{s}{c}.
$$

- Stronger selection $s$ ⟹ faster fixation ⟹ **deeper** valley (less time for recombination
  to rescue neutral variants).
- More recombination $c$ ⟹ **narrower** valley (neighbors escape the sweep).
- Diversity **recovers** with time $T$ after the sweep.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}
**FIGURE** — diversity valley: $\pi$ along a chromosome dipping at a swept site, with width
set by $s/c$; compare a recent vs. older sweep.
:::

## Hard, soft, and partial sweeps

- **Hard sweep** — a *single* new mutation fixes; one haplotype dominates ⟹ strongest signal.
- **Soft sweep** — selection on **standing variation** or recurrent mutation ⟹ *multiple*
  haplotypes carry the adaptive allele ⟹ weaker, harder-to-detect signal.
- **Partial sweep** — sampled before fixation (or selection relaxed) ⟹ adaptive allele at
  intermediate frequency.

::: {.callout-note}
Crop and local-adaptation alleles are often **soft** (selection on standing variation), so
classic hard-sweep scans can miss them. <span class="xref">→ deck 05.</span>
:::

## Computing Tajima's $D$ from an SFS

The sweep signature is an SFS skewed to **rare** variants. Compute $D$ directly from a
folded/unfolded spectrum:

```r
TajimaD <- function(sfs) {              # sfs = c(#singletons, #doubletons, ...)
  n  <- length(sfs) + 1                 # number of sampled chromosomes
  ss <- sum(sfs)                        # segregating sites
  a1 <- sum(1 / seq_len(n - 1)); a2 <- sum(1 / seq_len(n - 1)^2)
  b1 <- (n + 1) / (3 * (n - 1)); b2 <- 2 * (n^2 + n + 3) / (9 * n * (n - 1))
  c1 <- b1 - 1/a1; c2 <- b2 - (n + 2)/(a1 * n) + a2/a1^2
  e1 <- c1 / a1;  e2 <- c2 / (a1^2 + a2)
  theta_pi <- sum(sapply(seq_along(sfs), function(i) i*(n-i)*sfs[i])) / choose(n, 2)
  theta_w  <- ss / a1
  (theta_pi - theta_w) / sqrt(e1*ss + e2*ss*(ss-1))
}
```

::: {.notes}
From J. Yang's AGRO-932 Tajima's-D lab. Display-only; change ```` ```r ```` to ```` ```{r} ````
to run live.
:::

## Sweep vs. neutral — try it

```r
sweep   <- c(20, 2, 1, 1, 1)   # rare-variant excess  → D < 0
neutral <- c( 6, 1, 2, 2, 4)   # flatter spectrum     → D ≈ 0
TajimaD(sweep)     # strongly negative
TajimaD(neutral)   # near zero
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- The **sweep** SFS piles up singletons ⟹ $\pi \ll \theta_W$ ⟹ **negative** $D$.
- Change the counts and watch $D$ move — this is the engine behind the genome scans in deck 05.
:::

# Divergence & molecular evolution {.center}

## The neutral substitution rate

Zoom out from polymorphism to **divergence between species**. Each generation a site gains
$2N\nu$ new mutations; a **neutral** one fixes with probability $1/2N$. The substitution
rate is their product:

$$
k = \underbrace{2N\nu f_0}_{\text{new neutral mutations}} \times
    \underbrace{\frac{1}{2N}}_{\text{fixation prob}} = \nu f_0 = \mu .
$$

::: {.callout-important}
$k = \mu$: the neutral substitution rate **equals the mutation rate, independent of $N$** —
the basis of the **molecular clock** [@kimura1968]. (More mutations arise in big
populations, but each is less likely to fix; the two cancel.)
:::

## Fixation probabilities set the rate

$$
u_0 = \frac{1}{2N},\qquad
u_a \approx 2 s_a,\qquad
u_d \approx \frac{2 s_d}{1 - e^{-4 N s_d}} .
$$

So substitution rates differ by selection class:

$$
k_{\text{neutral}} = \mu,\qquad
k_{\text{adv}} = 4N\nu f_a s_a,\qquad
k_{\text{del}} = \frac{4N\nu f_d s_d}{1 - e^{-4N s_d}} .
$$

- Unlike neutral substitution, **selected** rates *do* depend on $N$ — selection is more
  effective in large populations.

## $d_N/d_S$ — detecting selection from divergence

Split coding divergence into **non-synonymous** ($d_N$) and **synonymous** ($d_S$). Taking
synonymous sites as neutral ($E[d_S] = 2t\nu$):

$$
\frac{d_N}{d_S} = f_0 + 4N f_a s_a + \frac{4N f_d s_d}{1 - e^{-4N s_d}} .
$$

| $d_N/d_S$ | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| $< 1$ | **purifying** selection (most genes — non-syn changes removed) |
| $\approx 1$ | neutral evolution |
| $> 1$ | **positive** selection (recurrent adaptive non-syn fixation) |

::: {.callout-note}
Within-species analog $\pi_N/\pi_S$ uses polymorphism instead of divergence; $\pi_N/\pi_S$
is usually $<1$ (purifying), and $>1$ hints at **balancing** selection.
:::

## Beyond Tajima: a toolbox

- **Fu & Li's $D$** — weights singletons (external branches) specifically.
- **Fay & Wu's $H$** — targets the **high-frequency derived** excess left by a sweep.
- **McDonald–Kreitman** — within- vs. between-species, syn vs. non-syn (run it on the
  deck-01 *Drosophila* ADH data!).
- **HKA** — polymorphism vs. divergence across loci.

<span class="xref">→ localized diversity loss around selected sites is the bridge to local
adaptation, deck 05.</span>

## Summary — key equations

$$
\mathbb E[\xi_i] = \frac{\theta}{i}
\qquad
D = \frac{\pi - \theta_W}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\pi - \theta_W)}}
\qquad
T_{\text{fix}} \approx \frac{2\ln(2N_e)}{s}
$$

$$
k = \mu \;\text{(neutral, } N\text{-independent)}
\qquad
\frac{d_N}{d_S} = f_0 + 4N f_a s_a + \dots
$$

- The **SFS** is a compressed genealogy; **Tajima's $D$** flags its skew (but is
  **ambiguous** alone — **genome-wide vs. local** separates demography from selection).
- **Linked selection** (sweeps, background selection) carves diversity **valleys**.
- Neutral substitution gives the **molecular clock** ($k=\mu$); $d_N/d_S$ reads selection
  from **divergence**.
